# Chapter 4: How to Make All Your Dreams Come True

## The Infomercial Setup

The chapter opens with a 2:00 a.m. infomercial scenario. The narrator appears on TV, shouting, “What if I told you that I could solve all your problems?” and “I know how to make all your dreams come true.” He claims to have once felt lost, alone, isolated, hopeless—statements that are “experienced by everybody” and “a fact of the human condition.” The pitch exploits the viewer’s crisis of hope: the Feeling Brain desperately craves salvation, and the Thinking Brain eventually concludes the idea is “so batshit crazy that it just might work.” The viewer grabs their phone, goes to the website, and signs up.

## Step One: Sell Hope to the Hopeless

Manson recounts a 2005 encounter in Boston, Massachusetts, with the LaRouche Youth Movement (LYM), a group started by far-left ideologue Lyndon LaRouche. Students held pictures of the 9/11 attacks with captions “America Deserved It,” and pamphlets depicting Dick Cheney with devil’s horns labeled “Mass Murderer” and George W. Bush with a Hitler mustache. When Manson argued, one student replied, “By participating in the system, you are perpetuating it, and therefore are complicit in the murder of millions of innocent civilians around the world. Here, read this.” Manson eventually left, quoting Carl Sagan: “I think your mind is so open your brain fell out!” No minds were changed.

The LYM is described as an “ideological religion” that preaches to disaffected college students: “It’s not your fault.” The message: if we could just overthrow “the system,” everything would be okay. Hope requires three components: values (a better future), self-control (capability to reach it), and community (shared support). Young adulthood is a period when many struggle with all three—crippling options, loss of authority figures, and need to find identity. For the first time, kids decide who to be; the options can be crippling. They are now responsible for their own decisions, and if they suck at getting out of bed or studying, there’s no one to blame but themselves. LaRouche capitalized on this: he gave a convoluted political explanation for disaffection, a sense of control through a plan to change the world, and a community where they “fit in.” Therefore, he gave them hope.

People are most impressionable when things are at their worst. When values fail, one religion falls and opens space for the next. “People who lose faith in their spiritual God will look for a worldly God. People who lose their family will give themselves away to their race, creed, or nation.” All major religions historically sent missionaries to the poorest and most destitute corners of the globe. Jim Jones built his following by recruiting the homeless and marginalized minorities with a socialist message mixed with Christianity. Jesus, Buddha, Moses—same approach. Today, social media makes it easy: post extreme content, let the algorithm do the rest.

## Step Two: Choose Your Faith

Faith is inevitable. “You pay your mortgage because you have faith that money is real.” There is no such thing as an atheist—everyone must believe, on faith, that something is important. Even nihilists believe on faith that nothing is more important than anything else. The highest value in the Feeling Brain’s hierarchy is the “God Value”—the lens through which all other values are interpreted. Examples: money (all conflict boils down to money), love (against anything that separates), Jesus/Muhammad/Buddha, oneself (narcissism), or another person (codependence). Narcissists and codependents often pair up in a “really sick and fucked-up way.”

Evidence belongs to the Thinking Brain; values are decided by the Feeling Brain. Evidence cannot verify values—they are subjective and arbitrary. A meteorite hitting a town: the traditional religious person says it happened because the town was full of sinners; the atheist says it’s proof there is no God; the hedonist decides to party more; the capitalist thinks about investing in meteorite-defense technologies. The only loophole is when evidence itself becomes the God Value—that is “science.”

Three types of religions based on God Value:

- **Spiritual religions**: draw hope from supernatural beliefs, looking for a better future outside this life. Examples: Christianity, Islam, Judaism, animism, Greek mythology. High risk/high reward—require most skill and charisma, but pay off in follower loyalty and longevity. Supernatural beliefs can never be proven or disproven, making them nearly impossible to dislodge. They encourage hope through death, making people willing to die for unverifiable beliefs.

- **Ideological religions**: draw hope from the natural world, looking for salvation in this life. Examples: capitalism, communism, environmentalism, liberalism, fascism, libertarianism. Play on “Normal Difficulty.” Verifiable to varying degrees, but still rely on faith because some things are impossible to test, and many ideologies require everyone to have faith in the same thing (e.g., money’s intrinsic value, national citizenship). Humans tend to take a little evidence and generalize—narcissism at work. Bad ideologies like racism persist due to ignorance far more than malice. In Manson’s lifetime alone there have been movements for LGBTQ rights, stem cell research, and decriminalizing drug use.

- **Interpersonal religions**: draw hope from other people. Examples: romantic love, children, sports heroes, political leaders, celebrities. Play on “Easy” mode—as common as people themselves. Sports are a form of religion: arbitrary value systems designed to give hope. Ted Williams is an American hero; other athletes are demonized for coming up short. Politics is an even grander example: entirely made-up positions of power exist only due to the faith of the population. Whether democracy or dictatorship, a small group of leaders is idolized or demonized. Fandom is low-level religion—fans of Will Smith, Katy Perry, or Elon Musk hang on every word. The most important interpersonal religions are familial and romantic relationships—each family is its own mini-church.

## Step Three: Preemptively Invalidate All Criticism

Create a self-reinforcing us-versus-them dichotomy so that anyone who criticizes “us” immediately becomes “them.” Examples: “If you don’t support the war, then you support the terrorists.” “God created science to test our faith in God.” “Anyone who criticizes feminism is sexist.” “Anyone who criticizes the president is a traitor.” “Anyone who thinks Kobe Bryant was better than Michael Jordan doesn’t understand basketball.” Common enemies create unity. “Some sort of scapegoat, whether justified or not, is necessary to blame for our pain and maintain our hope.” Conspiracy theories help: “It’s not just that vaccines cause autism; it’s that the medical and pharmaceutical industries are getting rich by destroying everyone’s families.” Or that climate change is a hoax created by the Chinese government to slow the U.S. economy. Or that pro-choicers are soldiers sent by Satan to destroy good Christian families.

## Step Four: Ritual Sacrifice

Rituals make values tangible. “You can’t think your way toward valuing something. You have to live it.” Manson recalls being forced to wear dress clothes to church as a kid, questioning why God cares what he wears on Sundays. Later he understood: dressing up signals to the community that “this Jesus stuff is serious business.” Robes appear at weddings, graduations, funerals, court hearings—visual cues of status and importance. Rituals are repeated over long periods, lending a sense of importance. They are symbolic—churches have guys in robes dipping bread in wine to represent Christ’s body. Countries create rituals around founding or wars. Married couples create inside jokes.

Rituals are usually about sacrifice. Newton’s First Law of Emotion: every action produces an equal and opposite emotional reaction. Finding a wallet with $100 and no ID—you keep it, cue guilt. You exist without deserving it—cue inherent guilt. Ancient sacrifices were enacted to repay that debt. Eventually, people realized you could symbolically sacrifice a life (Jesus’s) for salvation. “Most religious practices are developed for the alleviation of guilt.” Prayer is miniature guilt alleviation: “Thanks, God, for letting me exist, even though it sucks to be me sometimes.”

Ideological religions direct guilt toward service—right-wing ideologies toward protecting country and family, left-wing toward sacrificing for the greater good. Interpersonal religions use rituals like rings, gifts, anniversaries to make people feel they deserve to be loved. Marriage: you stand at an altar and promise to give your life to this other person.

## Step Five: Promise Heaven, Deliver Hell

The more you promise salvation, the more followers fail to live up to it, blame themselves, feel guilty, and do whatever you tell them to make up for it. Some call this the cycle of psychological abuse. Pyramid schemes do this: you give a scumbag money for products nobody wants, fail to sell them, blame yourself—because the guy at the top has a Ferrari, so the problem must be you. Seminars psych you up with music and chants (“Winners never give up! Losers believe it won’t work for them!”) but don’t teach you how to sell anything. The same cycle plays out in fitness plans, political activism, self-help, financial planning, even visiting your grandmother on a holiday.

“Human pain is like a game of Whac-A-Mole. Every time you knock down one kind of pain, another one pops up. And the faster you whack them, the faster they come back.” There is no end to the pain moles. Leaders need followers to be perpetually dissatisfied—it’s good for business. “If someone really could solve all your problems, they’d go out of business by next Tuesday.” No religion will make you feel blissful all the time. No country will feel completely fair. True equality can never be achieved. True freedom doesn’t exist. “There are no solutions, only stopgap measures, only incremental improvements, only slightly better forms of fuckedness than others.” This is our fucked-up world, and we’re the fucked-up ones in it.

## Step Six: Prophet for Profit

With a following, you can have anything: a dozen sex slaves (make up scripture about “Stage Six of Manatee Enlightenment”), a huge piece of land (tell followers only you can build paradise), power and prestige (vote you into office or overthrow the government). “You just have to trample on the hopes and dreams of thousands of other people to get there.”

But you’re already in a religion. “If you think you’re above religion, that you use logic and reason, I’m sorry to say, you’re wrong: you are one of us.” Religions compete in a Darwinian fashion; those with the most efficient value hierarchies win out and become the foundation for culture. But every time a religion succeeds, its God Value shifts to preservation of the religion itself. “This is how you go from Jesus to the Crusades, from Marxism to the gulags, from a wedding chapel to divorce court.” Success is more precarious than failure because “by experiencing our hopes, we lose them.” The only thing that can truly destroy a dream is to have it come true.

The narrator appears on TV, shouting, “What if I told you that I could solve all your problems?” and “I know how to make all your dreams come true.” He claims to have once felt lost, alone, isolated, hopeless—statements that are “experienced by everybody” and “a fact of the human condition.” The pitch exploits the viewer’s crisis of hope: the Feeling Brain desperately craves salvation, and the Thinking Brain eventually concludes the idea is “so batshit crazy that it just might work.” The viewer grabs their phone, goes to the website, and signs up.

## Step One: Sell Hope to the Hopeless

Manson recounts a 2005 encounter in Boston, Massachusetts, with the LaRouche Youth Movement (LYM), a group started by far-left ideologue Lyndon LaRouche. Students held pictures of the 9/11 attacks with captions “America Deserved It,” and pamphlets depicting Dick Cheney with devil’s horns labeled “Mass Murderer” and George W. Bush with a Hitler mustache. When Manson argued, one student replied, “By participating in the system, you are perpetuating it, and therefore are complicit in the murder of millions of innocent civilians around the world. Here, read this.” Manson eventually left, quoting Carl Sagan: “I think your mind is so open your brain fell out!” No minds were changed.

The LYM is described as an “ideological religion” that preaches to disaffected college students: “It’s not your fault.” The message: if we could just overthrow “the system,” everything would be okay. Hope requires three components: values (a better future), self-control (capability to reach it), and community (shared support). Young adulthood is a period when many struggle with all three—crippling options, loss of authority figures, and need to find identity. For the first time, kids decide who to be; the options can be crippling. They are now responsible for their own decisions, and if they suck at getting out of bed or studying, there’s no one to blame but themselves. LaRouche capitalized on this: he gave a convoluted political explanation for disaffection, a sense of control through a plan to change the world, and a community where they “fit in.” Therefore, he gave them hope.

People are most impressionable when things are at their worst. When values fail, one religion falls and opens space for the next. “People who lose faith in their spiritual God will look for a worldly God. People who lose their family will give themselves away to their race, creed, or nation.” All major religions historically sent missionaries to the poorest and most destitute corners of the globe. Jim Jones built his following by recruiting the homeless and marginalized minorities with a socialist message mixed with Christianity. Jesus, Buddha, Moses—same approach. Today, social media makes it easy: post extreme content, let the algorithm do the rest.

## Step Two: Choose Your Faith

Faith is inevitable. “You pay your mortgage because you have faith that money is real.” There is no such thing as an atheist—everyone must believe, on faith, that something is important. Even nihilists believe on faith that nothing is more important than anything else. The highest value in the Feeling Brain’s hierarchy is the “God Value”—the lens through which all other values are interpreted. Examples: money (all conflict boils down to money), love (against anything that separates), Jesus/Muhammad/Buddha, oneself (narcissism), or another person (codependence). Narcissists and codependents often pair up in a “really sick and fucked-up way.”

Evidence belongs to the Thinking Brain; values are decided by the Feeling Brain. Evidence cannot verify values—they are subjective and arbitrary. A meteorite hitting a town: the traditional religious person says it happened because the town was full of sinners; the atheist says it’s proof there is no God; the hedonist decides to party more; the capitalist thinks about investing in meteorite-defense technologies. The only loophole is when evidence itself becomes the God Value—that is “science.”

Three types of religions based on God Value:

- **Spiritual religions**: draw hope from supernatural beliefs, looking for a better future outside this life. Examples: Christianity, Islam, Judaism, animism, Greek mythology. High risk/high reward—require most skill and charisma, but pay off in follower loyalty and longevity. Supernatural beliefs can never be proven or disproven, making them nearly impossible to dislodge. They encourage hope through death, making people willing to die for unverifiable beliefs.

- **Ideological religions**: draw hope from the natural world, looking for salvation in this life. Examples: capitalism, communism, environmentalism, liberalism, fascism, libertarianism. Play on “Normal Difficulty.” Verifiable to varying degrees, but still rely on faith because some things are impossible to test, and many ideologies require everyone to have faith in the same thing (e.g., money’s intrinsic value, national citizenship). Humans tend to take a little evidence and generalize—narcissism at work. Bad ideologies like racism persist due to ignorance far more than malice. In Manson’s lifetime alone there have been movements for LGBTQ rights, stem cell research, and decriminalizing drug use.

- **Interpersonal religions**: draw hope from other people. Examples: romantic love, children, sports heroes, political leaders, celebrities. Play on “Easy” mode—as common as people themselves. Sports are a form of religion: arbitrary value systems designed to give hope. Ted Williams is an American hero; other athletes are demonized for coming up short. Politics is an even grander example: entirely made-up positions of power exist only due to the faith of the population. Whether democracy or dictatorship, a small group of leaders is idolized or demonized. Fandom is low-level religion—fans of Will Smith, Katy Perry, or Elon Musk hang on every word. The most important interpersonal religions are familial and romantic relationships—each family is its own mini-church.

## Step Three: Preemptively Invalidate All Criticism

Create a self-reinforcing us-versus-them dichotomy so that anyone who criticizes “us” immediately becomes “them.” Examples: “If you don’t support the war, then you support the terrorists.” “God created science to test our faith in God.” “Anyone who criticizes feminism is sexist.” “Anyone who criticizes the president is a traitor.” “Anyone who thinks Kobe Bryant was better than Michael Jordan doesn’t understand basketball.” Common enemies create unity. “Some sort of scapegoat, whether justified or not, is necessary to blame for our pain and maintain our hope.” Conspiracy theories help: “It’s not just that vaccines cause autism; it’s that the medical and pharmaceutical industries are getting rich by destroying everyone’s families.” Or that climate change is a hoax created by the Chinese government to slow the U.S. economy. Or that pro-choicers are soldiers sent by Satan to destroy good Christian families.

## Step Four: Ritual Sacrifice

Rituals make values tangible. “You can’t think your way toward valuing something. You have to live it.” Manson recalls being forced to wear dress clothes to church as a kid, questioning why God cares what he wears on Sundays. Later he understood: dressing up signals to the community that “this Jesus stuff is serious business.” Robes appear at weddings, graduations, funerals, court hearings—visual cues of status and importance. Rituals are repeated over long periods, lending a sense of importance. They are symbolic—churches have guys in robes dipping bread in wine to represent Christ’s body. Countries create rituals around founding or wars. Married couples create inside jokes.

Rituals are usually about sacrifice. Newton’s First Law of Emotion: every action produces an equal and opposite emotional reaction. Finding a wallet with $100 and no ID—you keep it, cue guilt. You exist without deserving it—cue inherent guilt. Ancient sacrifices were enacted to repay that debt. Eventually, people realized you could symbolically sacrifice a life (Jesus’s) for salvation. “Most religious practices are developed for the alleviation of guilt.” Prayer is miniature guilt alleviation: “Thanks, God, for letting me exist, even though it sucks to be me sometimes.”

Ideological religions direct guilt toward service—right-wing ideologies toward protecting country and family, left-wing toward sacrificing for the greater good. Interpersonal religions use rituals like rings, gifts, anniversaries to make people feel they deserve to be loved. Marriage: you stand at an altar and promise to give your life to this other person.

## Step Five: Promise Heaven, Deliver Hell

The more you promise salvation, the more followers fail to live up to it, blame themselves, feel guilty, and do whatever you tell them to make up for it. Some call this the cycle of psychological abuse. Pyramid schemes do this: you give a scumbag money for products nobody wants, fail to sell them, blame yourself—because the guy at the top has a Ferrari, so the problem must be you. Seminars psych you up with music and chants (“Winners never give up! Losers believe it won’t work for them!”) but don’t teach you how to sell anything. The same cycle plays out in fitness plans, political activism, self-help, financial planning, even visiting your grandmother on a holiday.

“Human pain is like a game of Whac-A-Mole. Every time you knock down one kind of pain, another one pops up. And the faster you whack them, the faster they come back.” There is no end to the pain moles. Leaders need followers to be perpetually dissatisfied—it’s good for business. “If someone really could solve all your problems, they’d go out of business by next Tuesday.” No religion will make you feel blissful all the time. No country will feel completely fair. True equality can never be achieved. True freedom doesn’t exist. “There are no solutions, only stopgap measures, only incremental improvements, only slightly better forms of fuckedness than others.” This is our fucked-up world, and we’re the fucked-up ones in it.

## Step Six: Prophet for Profit

With a following, you can have anything: a dozen sex slaves (make up scripture about “Stage Six of Manatee Enlightenment”), a huge piece of land (tell followers only you can build paradise), power and prestige (vote you into office or overthrow the government). “You just have to trample on the hopes and dreams of thousands of other people to get there.”

But you’re already in a religion. “If you think you’re above religion, that you use logic and reason, I’m sorry to say, you’re wrong: you are one of us.” Religions compete in a Darwinian fashion; those with the most efficient value hierarchies win out and become the foundation for culture. But every time a religion succeeds, its God Value shifts to preservation of the religion itself. “This is how you go from Jesus to the Crusades, from Marxism to the gulags, from a wedding chapel to divorce court.” Success is more precarious than failure because “by experiencing our hopes, we lose them.” The only thing that can truly destroy a dream is to have it come true.
